name: Pasighat
tagline: Adi country where the Siang meets the plains
meta_description: Pasighat travel guide: the Siang river, Adi villages, Solung in September, Daying Ering sanctuary, real costs and how to reach from Dibrugarh via Bogibeel.
summary: Pasighat is the headquarters of East Siang district, set at about 155 m where the Siang leaves the hills for the Assam plains. Founded in 1911, it is the oldest town in Arunachal and the heart of Adi country. Stay 2 nights for the river, Adi villages and Daying Ering sanctuary.
intro: Pasighat sits on the right bank of the Siang, the river the Tibetans call the Yarlung Tsangpo and the Assamese know as the Brahmaputra once it reaches the plains. Here the Siang comes out of a deep valley into a wide braided bed of sand and islands. The town grew from a British administrative post set up in 1911, which makes it the oldest town in Arunachal Pradesh.

This is Adi country. Adi villages of bamboo and timber houses on stilts surround the town, with community halls called mosup or dere, rice fields and orange and areca gardens. The indigenous Donyi-Polo faith, worship of the Sun and Moon, is practised alongside Christianity, and the great festival of the year is Solung, celebrated from 1 September with dances, songs and apong rice beer.

Pasighat is also a gateway. Dibrugarh in Assam is now close thanks to the Bogibeel bridge, and roads lead north to Aalo and Mechuka, east to Roing, and up the Siang to Yingkiong. It is low and warm, so October to March is the comfortable season. Use it to rest after the hills, to watch the river at sunset and to visit Adi villages with a local guide.
facts: Dibrugarh (≈ 100 km via Bogibeel); Pasighat airport has limited flights
Siang river, Adi villages, Solung festival, Daying Ering sanctuary

highlights.title: Sunset over the Siang
highlights.text: Walk down to the river ghats on the edge of town in the late afternoon. The Siang spreads into channels and sandbanks below the last hills, boats cross to the islands, and in winter the water turns a clear green-blue.

highlights.title: Daying Ering Wildlife Sanctuary
highlights.text: About 13 km from town, this sanctuary protects river islands, grassland and riverine forest in the Siang. In winter, migratory ducks and waders join resident birds; entry and boat crossings need forest department permission.

highlights.title: Adi villages and the mosup
highlights.text: Villages around Pasighat keep stilt houses, granaries and the mosup, a community hall where young people traditionally gathered and village matters were discussed. Visit with a local guide who can introduce you to families.

highlights.title: Solung in September
highlights.text: From 1 September the Adi celebrate Solung, an agricultural festival with ritual offerings, the ponung dance by women and evenings of song and apong. Pasighat holds public celebrations alongside the village rituals.

highlights.title: Gateway to the Siang valley
highlights.text: Pasighat is the base for drives north to Aalo, Mechuka and Yingkiong, and east to Roing. Arrange Sumo seats and permits here, and stock up on cash before heading into the hills.

field_notes.fact: Pasighat was founded by the British in 1911 as an administrative post, making it the oldest town in Arunachal Pradesh. It is the headquarters of East Siang district and sits at about 155 m on the Siang.

The Bogibeel Bridge across the Brahmaputra near Dibrugarh, opened in December 2018, is India's longest combined rail and road bridge at about 4.94 km. It cut the road journey from Dibrugarh to Pasighat to a few hours.
Daying Ering Wildlife Sanctuary near Pasighat covers islands, grasslands and riverine forest in the Siang. It was declared a sanctuary in 1986 and is known for wintering water birds.

costs: Taxi for a half day around town and villages

how_to_reach.text: Dibrugarh airport, with flights from Delhi, Kolkata and Guwahati, is the usual gateway, about 100 km and 2.5–3 hours away via the Bogibeel bridge. Pasighat's own airport has had limited regional flights; check current status before you travel.

Shared Sumos run from Dibrugarh and Itanagar to Pasighat, and buses connect Pasighat with Itanagar. Murkongselek in Assam, about 30 km away, is the nearest railhead with a few trains; Dibrugarh has many more.

From Dibrugarh, cross the Bogibeel bridge and drive through Dhemaji district to Ruksin and Pasighat. From Itanagar the trans-Arunachal road takes about 6–8 hours. The Inner Line Permit is checked at the Ruksin gate.

where_to_stay: Saver: simple hotels and lodges in town charge about ₹1,500–2,500 a night for a double; some villages near Pasighat have homestays that a local guide can arrange. Comfort: a handful of mid-range hotels in town have clean rooms with attached bathrooms and hot water, which is what our comfort trips use. Signature: Pasighat has no luxury hotel. On signature trips we use the best room available here and keep the focus on private guiding and time on the river.
tips: Book Sumo seats to Aalo or Mechuka a day ahead at the town counters; morning departures fill first.
List East Siang and any other district you will enter on your Inner Line Permit; it is checked at Ruksin.
Visit Adi villages with a local guide and ask before entering a mosup or photographing rituals.
Carry cash from Dibrugarh or Pasighat before heading north; ATMs thin out quickly.
Plan Daying Ering for winter mornings, when birds are on the islands and the river is low.

experiences.title: Sunset on the Siang at Pasighat
experiences.summary: Watch the Siang spread out of the hills into braided channels and sandbanks as the sun sets behind the ridges, with boats crossing to the islands and families on the ghats.
body: Few places show the change from mountain river to plains river as clearly as Pasighat. Upstream, the Siang has come from Tibet through one of the deepest gorges on earth. Below the town it spreads into channels, islands and sand. From the river ghats on the edge of town you can see both: the last forested hills to the north and the open, braided bed running south towards Assam.

Go in the late afternoon between October and March, when the water is low and clear and the light turns gold. Local families picnic on the sand and fishermen work the shallows. Where boatmen are operating, you can cross to a nearby island for a short ride; agree the price first and wear a life jacket if one is offered.

The current is strong even in winter, so do not wade far or swim. In the monsoon the river rises dramatically and the ghats may be closed. Carry water, a light jacket for the evening and a torch for the walk back, and take any rubbish with you.

faqs.q: Where is the best place to watch the Siang in Pasighat?
faqs.a: The river ghats on the edge of town are the easiest, with open views of the braided channels and hills. Ask locally for the current access point, since sandbanks shift each year.

faqs.q: Can I take a boat on the Siang at Pasighat?
faqs.a: Boatmen sometimes take visitors across to islands in the dry season for ₹100–500. Agree the price first, wear a life jacket where available, and avoid boats in high water.

faqs.q: Is the Siang the same as the Brahmaputra?
faqs.a: Yes. The river is the Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibet, the Siang in Arunachal and, after it joins the Dibang and Lohit in Assam, the Brahmaputra.

experiences.title: Birding in Daying Ering sanctuary
experiences.cost: Vehicle ₹2,000–3,500; forest entry, boat and guide fees extra
experiences.summary: Cross to the river islands of the Siang to look for wintering ducks, waders and grassland birds in a sanctuary of sandbars, tall grass and riverine forest, 13 km from town.
body: Daying Ering Wildlife Sanctuary protects a stretch of the Siang's islands, channels, grasslands and patches of riverine forest close to Pasighat. Declared in 1986, it is one of the few protected wetland and grassland habitats in Arunachal, and in winter it draws migratory ducks, waders and raptors alongside resident river birds. Hog deer and wild pig live in the grass.

Access is by road to the sanctuary edge and then by boat to the islands, so you need permission from the forest department in Pasighat and usually a forest staff member or local guide. Go early: leave town around 6 am to be on the water when birds are most active. Bring binoculars, a long lens if you have one, water and snacks.

Facilities are basic, and arrangements vary from year to year with river levels and staffing. Ask at the forest office a day ahead, and check current status before you travel. Keep voices low, stay on the paths your guide shows you, and take all rubbish back to town.

faqs.q: How do I visit Daying Ering Wildlife Sanctuary?
faqs.a: Get permission from the forest department in Pasighat, then drive about 13 km to the sanctuary and cross by boat with forest staff or a local guide. Arrangements change with river levels, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What birds can I see at Daying Ering?
faqs.a: In winter, migratory ducks, waders and raptors join resident river birds such as kingfishers, cormorants and egrets. Grassland species live in the tall grass. Sightings vary each year.

faqs.q: When is the best season for Daying Ering?
faqs.a: November to March, when migratory birds are present and the river is low. The monsoon brings floods that cover much of the sanctuary.

experiences.title: An Adi village, the mosup and apong
experiences.summary: Visit an Adi village near Pasighat with a local guide: stilt houses, granaries, the mosup community hall, orange and areca gardens, and a cup of apong if your hosts offer one.
body: The Adi are one of the largest communities of Arunachal, living mainly along the Siang and its tributaries. Villages near Pasighat are built of timber and bamboo, with houses raised on stilts, granaries set slightly apart, and a mosup or dere, the community hall at the centre of village life. Around them are rice fields, orange orchards and areca and bamboo groves.

Go with a local guide, who can arrange a welcome, explain the kebang, the traditional village council, and introduce you to families. Many Adi follow Donyi-Polo, worship of the Sun and Moon, and you may see small shrines or ritual offerings. If you are offered apong, the rice beer brewed at home and served in bamboo or gourd vessels, a sip is polite; it is fine to decline.

Remove your shoes where your hosts do, ask before photographing people or rituals, and do not enter a mosup or shrine unless invited. A small contribution or gift for the household that hosts you is welcome. If you are here from 1 September, Solung brings dancing and feasting to many villages.

faqs.q: What is a mosup in an Adi village?
faqs.a: A mosup or dere is the community hall of an Adi village. It was traditionally a dormitory for young men and a place for the village council to meet, and it is still used for gatherings and festivals.

Apong is rice beer brewed at home by the Adi and Mising, often in a light version and a stronger smoked version. It is offered to guests and at festivals. Taking a small sip is polite; you can also decline.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide to visit Adi villages near Pasighat?
faqs.a: We strongly recommend one. A local guide can arrange a welcome, explain customs and keep you away from ritual spaces at sensitive times. Expect ₹1,000–2,000 for the day.

faqs.q: How do I reach Pasighat from Dibrugarh?
faqs.a: Cross the Bogibeel bridge and drive about 100 km through Dhemaji district, roughly 2.5–3 hours by car. Shared Sumos run for about ₹300–500 a seat. The Inner Line Permit is checked at the Ruksin gate on the state border.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Pasighat?
faqs.a: Yes. Indian visitors need an Inner Line Permit listing East Siang district, and foreign nationals need a Protected Area Permit. List any other districts you plan to visit, such as West Siang or Shi Yomi for Mechuka. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When is the Solung festival in Pasighat?
faqs.a: Solung usually begins on 1 September and runs for several days, with public celebrations in Pasighat and rituals and dances in villages. Exact programmes vary by village each year, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Pasighat?
faqs.a: October to March, when the weather is warm and dry and the river is low. September is wet but has Solung. April and May get hot, and June to August bring heavy rain and road damage across the Siang valley.

faqs.q: How many days do I need in Pasighat?
faqs.a: Two nights is enough for the river, an Adi village and Daying Ering sanctuary. Many travellers spend one night here on the way to or from Mechuka, which is a long day's drive north.

faqs.q: Is Pasighat a good base for Mechuka?
faqs.a: Yes. It is the usual gateway: shared Sumos and private cars run north to Aalo in about 3–4 hours and on to Mechuka, about 280 km and 10–11 hours from Pasighat in all. Many travellers break the journey at Aalo.

faqs.q: Are there ATMs and mobile network in Pasighat?
faqs.a: Yes. Pasighat has several ATMs and 4G from major networks. North of Aalo, ATMs are fewer and signal weaker, so draw enough cash here for Mechuka.

faqs.q: What food should I try in Pasighat?
faqs.a: Try Adi dishes of rice with pork, chicken or river fish cooked with bamboo shoot and local herbs, smoked meat, and apong rice beer where offered. Simple restaurants in town also serve North Indian food and momos.
Yes, it is a calm district town used to visitors. Take care on the river, where the current is strong, and on roads after dark. In the monsoon, landslides and floods can cut roads for days.
